heading: Training data and setup affect induction heads and how long in-context learning lasts
definition: whether and when induction heads form, and whether in-context learning persists, depends on properties of the training data and setup.
summary: Several independent groups find that training data and setup affect induction-head formation or how long in-context learning lasts, including controlled interventions in Pythia-14M–160M and a 1.485B decoder. Effects depend on the property and task: in one synthetic task, varying depth across 6, 12 and 18 layers had no consistent effect on how long in-context learning lasted.

suggested_status.by_scale: toy: R2 (synthetic classification in arXiv:2312.03002#R10–R13); scope limit in a synthetic exemplar-label task (parameter count not given in the pack): depth of 6/12/18 layers has no consistent effect on ICL transience (arXiv:2311.08360#r2–r4; labelled challenges for depth dependence only). <1B: R2 (controlled Pythia-14M–160M data interventions in arXiv:2601.21996#R5–R8); arXiv:2205.10487 contributes R1 evidence because it shares authors with an original. 1-10B: R2 for tested from-scratch interventions at 1.485B (arXiv:2609.32991#R40); its teacher-time comparison uses a 350M selector proxy and 1.485B target (arXiv:2609.32991#R25–R28). Extension to 7–9B remains unestablished by the removed endpoint comparisons. 10-100B: ? (counts: versions.V5.coverage_by_operation.training.by_size has no 10-100B). >100B: ? (no coverage in counts: versions.V5.studies_by_size).
suggested_status.reason: R2 remains appropriate for dependence on some data or setup properties: targeted deletion or augmentation changes induction emergence relative to matched random controls in Pythia-14M–160M (arXiv:2601.21996#R5, arXiv:2601.21996#R6, arXiv:2601.21996#R7, arXiv:2601.21996#R8); synthetic classification varies with class count, burstiness and within-class variation (arXiv:2312.03002#R10, arXiv:2312.03002#R11, arXiv:2312.03002#R12); curriculum changes formation trajectories in a 1.485B decoder (arXiv:2609.32991#R40). Repeated-subset training also supports data dependence, including substantial prefix-matching damage at 50% repetition; it supplies R1 evidence because its header identifies shared authors with an original (arXiv:2205.10487#r1, arXiv:2205.10487#r2). Teacher-time and order effects qualify intervention strength: induction-AUC changes are small and direction-dependent, without uncertainty for these contrasts; their target is 1.485B, not 160M (arXiv:2609.32991#R25, arXiv:2609.32991#R26, arXiv:2609.32991#R27, arXiv:2609.32991#R28). Counts: versions.V5.verdicts.supports.studies = 45, versions.V5.verdicts.limits_scope.studies = 13, versions.V5.verdicts.challenges.studies = 0, and versions.V5.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 1 are supplied pre-correction totals, not recomputed verdict totals. One condition-specific challenge is recorded (V5.against[2]): in a synthetic exemplar-label task with two seeds, depth of 6, 12 or 18 layers has no consistent effect on ICL transience (arXiv:2311.08360#r2, arXiv:2311.08360#r3, arXiv:2311.08360#r4). The pack's verdict on these rows is limits_scope ('not every setup property matters'); the checker relabelled it challenges, so versions.V5.verdicts.challenges.studies = 0 predates that relabel. The same study reports that other data and setup properties change whether ICL emerges or how it persists: class count (arXiv:2311.08360#r8), Zipf skew, where exponent 2 prevents ICL from emerging (arXiv:2311.08360#r13), L2 regularisation (arXiv:2311.08360#r15) and embedding width (arXiv:2311.08360#r20). The depth result is not a failed replication of the dependences above, and it does not argue that they are artifacts. Those are the two grounds for C in the README scale, so it is recorded here as a scope limit on R2, not as C.
suggested_status.open_questions: Controlled from-scratch data manipulations at ≥7B would establish whether the supported scale range extends upward. Matched tests of head formation and token-index ICL persistence during natural-language pretraining would clarify which outcomes depend on data. Independent replication of repeated-subset interventions would strengthen that currently R1 evidence. Evidence that the independent formation effects fail under matched conditions or arise from measurement artifacts could change the overall level. The level also depends on the single rule Iris sets for condition-specific challenges across all versions. If any challenges label gives C for its own condition, V5 reads C for depth dependence of ICL transience in synthetic exemplar-label tasks (arXiv:2311.08360#r2–r4) and R2 elsewhere. Under the README definition of C applied here, it stays R2 with that scope limit.

original_result.setup: The original study trained models with “smeared keys”: each attention key mixed information from the current and previous tokens using a trainable mixing weight.
original_result.result: Using smeared keys enabled the transition to in-context learning in one-layer models and made that transition occur earlier in models with two or more layers.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: NormSoftmax improved in-context accuracy and appeared to prevent failed learning transitions on Omniglot.
Statistics of trigger tokens changed learning speed; how outputs were distributed changed in-context generalization.
Synthetic data properties determined whether in-context learning emerged reliably.
Multi-token prediction improved small-model induction, while adding books accelerated and strengthened induction.
Learning rate and dropout advanced copying onset, while regularization improved final accuracy.
Data, regularization and embeddings changed the emergence and persistence of in-context learning.
Task parameters and optimization changed plateau duration in the toy model.
Training-data repetition switched ELIZA between copying by token content and copying by position.
Positional encoding changed how completely previous-token and induction heads formed.
Removing single-token frequency cues eliminated the long period of stalled learning in Markov-chain training.
Noise, context relevance and memorization training changed in-context learning and its persistence.
More classes or labels delayed the induction phase change through different subcircuits.
Chain-of-thought supervision produced induction heads where binary supervision produced a counting shortcut.
Distillation from an imperfect teacher reduced induction-task accuracy in small transformers.
Greater data diversity favored induction over positional shortcuts and improved out-of-distribution accuracy.
Masking induction-predictable positions reduced strong induction heads and made their emergence gradual.
Pythia learned to copy frequent tokens earlier and faster.
Suppressing syntactic attention delayed and weakened induction-head formation in GPT2.
Markov-chain induction heads required enough training transition matrices, large hidden dimensions and suitable encodings.
In the idealized model, induction emergence time grew with the square of context length.
Context, repetition and dependency reliability determined induction-head emergence across language and synthetic data.
Training on transitive inference from adjacent pairs formed induction circuits; linear-regression pretraining did not.
Architecture, data and training history changed in-context learning emergence and persistence in small models.
Repetition accelerated associative-recall emergence, but excessive repetition favored solutions that failed to generalize.
Upweighting induction-pattern tokens delayed or accelerated formation depending on training stage.
Curricula using text-copying snippets changed induction-head organization and reduced in-context performance in a 1B model.
Token noise and larger transition perturbations degraded Markov induction performance and attention alignment.
Exact instance copies enabled induction-related circuits and in-context learning across natural datasets.
Data, architecture and optimization changed induction emergence.
Multimodal in-context learning depended on data statistics, when modalities were combined, and positional encoding.
Positional schemes and spectral constraints shifted induction timing without preventing formation.
Task difficulty and optimization settings delayed induction emergence or prevented convergence.
Hierarchical data produced induction scores; matched flat data did not.
Masked diffusion models transitioned earlier than matched autoregressive models.
Targeted training-data deletion delayed induction emergence, while targeted augmentation accelerated it.
Induction-pattern token weighting controlled induction-head formation, strength and number.
A repeated-token data mix triggered induction that otherwise never emerged.
Instruction tuning shifted Mistral-7B retrieval toward the token following a match.
Gradual fading enabled retrieval with gates at zero where alternative training paths failed.
Curriculum and teacher scheduling improved selective matching.
More training sources worsened transient in-context loss increases and slowed synchronization.
SpiritLM showed lower prefix-matching scores than Llama-2-7B in preliminary comparisons.
Theory linked induction-learning gradients to bursty data and saturation of learning through model-weight updates.
Hybrid architecture and training choices changed induction-circuit location, timing and recall performance.
Repeated-data training disproportionately degraded prefix matching, copying and in-context learning near the double-descent peak.
Multi-token prediction lost its induction advantage at 100M nonembedding parameters and above on children stories.
Model depth had no consistent effect on in-context learning transience.
Increasing label count did not consistently delay the phase change across seeds.
Induction metrics disagreed under high repetition in synthetic data.
Text-copying snippet curricula gave in-context performance comparable to training on natural text alone in smaller models.
Small transition perturbations preserved near-ideal induction attention and similar loss.
Induction eventually formed despite severe masking, with comparable final scores across training regimes.
Instruction tuning changed mean induction scores little in Llama, Qwen and Gemma.
GPT-2 retained its established circuit after continued training on a similar corpus.
Gradual fading only slightly improved linear-regression learning over training with gates fixed at zero.
Teacher and ordering interventions produced small, mixed effects on induction and ambiguous recall.
Induction-enriched text barely changed onset, and some hybrid interventions had inconsistent effects.
Preferential prefix-matching damage varied across repeated-data fractions.

untested.what: No study tests whether ICL in V3's sense (loss falling with token index) persists or fades during natural-language pretraining under different data. Other persistence measurements concern few-shot accuracy in synthetic classification and context-following after one fine-tune (2410.23042). In Karpathy GPT-2 124M, switching from FineWeb-10B at step 17600 to 8000 OWT continuation steps (about 0.5B tokens) preserves the established ≥50×-selectivity head set (Jaccard 1.00; 5 shared, 0 FineWeb-only), continuous elevated PR and approximately constant induction selectivity. This experiment tests neither formation nor ICL-performance persistence and receives no V5 verdict.

wording_issues.phrase: whether and when induction heads form
wording_issues.issue: Timing changes need not change final head presence. Pythia pretraining regimes converge to comparable saturation, and heads form with 95% of formation-window samples masked (2601.21996). Heads form under every tested copy curriculum (2509.22947). The positional and spectral interventions in 2607.06621 are two-layer attention-only toy experiments on a per-sequence random-map task: every arm shows strong previous-token and induction behavior, while formation timing varies. These detector results do not establish the composition mechanism or dependence of final head presence on setup. By contrast, Repress-0x almost entirely prevents head formation in a 3M model (2601.13548).

Supporting behavioral comparisons do not always measure head formation. 2311.08360 and 2410.23042 list head formation as untested. In 2409.09281, batch-size, learning-rate and regularization comparisons report copying accuracy rather than corresponding head-score comparisons; a separate analysis defines induction score I(L,H) and tracks it across checkpoints of a single model. 2404.19737 uses a behavioral proxy. These behavioral outcomes need to be distinguished from direct measurements of head formation.

Persistence results use task-specific evaluators rather than V3's token-index loss. 2311.08360 randomly reassigns exemplar-class labels to 0 and 1. 2410.23042 measures 0-1 error with cyclically shifted labels within existing classes; its additional held-out-image evaluation also uses existing classes. 2503.05631 replaces training labels with 0 and 1, restricts in-context accuracy to the context labels, and also assesses persistence with the Flip evaluator. These are not uniformly held-out-class evaluations. Gemini Nano 1 follows context 8/8 before a memorisation fine-tune and 4/8 afterward, demonstrating training dependence without complete loss of context-following (2410.23042). GPT-2 124M circuit identity persists after a FineWeb→OWT switch, but this measures neither head formation nor ICL-performance persistence (2605.24059).

wording_issues.phrase: properties of the training data and setup
wording_issues.issue: The phrase is broad enough to cover architecture (positional schemes, convolution, NormSoftmax, MLPs), optimiser, objective, regularisation and post-training. The verdict fix on the original's only V5 row (smeared keys) says it bears on V5 only if 'training setup' includes architecture. A verdict fix in 2609.32991 notes that V5 'sets no direction', so almost any change counts as support.

Dependence should be stated for the tested property and outcome. Across 6/12/18-layer models, 2311.08360 finds no consistent depth effect on transience and similar decay slopes; this challenges depth dependence only. In the two-layer single-head Markov-task transformer of 2508.07208, transition perturbation α=0.1 gives a loss gap of 0.101 ± 0.003 versus 0.100 ± 0.003 at α=0.0; no significance or equivalence test establishes zero dependence or a precise threshold. Modest base-versus-instruct endpoint score differences in Llama, Qwen and Gemma do not measure formation, timing or ICL persistence (2604.01094). Unchanged established circuit identity after a similar-corpus switch likewise leaves those V5 outcomes undetermined (2605.24059).

One property can push 'whether' and 'when' in opposite directions. More classes promote ICL over IWL (2312.03002), and 1600 classes with 5 exemplars gives no ICL (2503.05631), yet more classes delay the phase change (2404.07129). Repetition likewise speeds emergence but in excess yields non-generalising solutions (2505.17863).

method_sensitivity.what: On −D data at 0.9-0.9, prefix matching shows no heads while logit attribution and associative recall show induction-like behaviour; dependence of the formation conclusion on measurement choice is observed (2511.16893). SWA Matching window 2 crosses thresholds 0.1/0.25/0.5/1 in (1, 2]K; window 8 crosses 0.1/0.25 in (1, 2]K and 0.5/1 in (2, 3]K (2609.15545). Teacher and order effects on induction AUC change direction with the teacher. The teacher-time evidence map identifies a 350M selector proxy and 1.485B target (2609.32991).

A batch-size effect read in update steps can flip in tokens. 2511.16893 reports that its shifting effect reverses direction in tokens (pack 'not in rows' line). 2409.09281 finds copying onset fixed in update steps across batch sizes, so it moves in tokens, and reports its dropout effect in tokens (15B → 10B).

Size changes whether an intervention matters, in opposite directions across studies. The training-objective effect on induction appears at ≤30M and disappears at ≥100M (2404.19737). Copy-snippet curricula change 10-shot ICL only at 1B (14.7–15.2 vs 20.0) and not at 0.13B or 0.5B (2509.22947).

In the minimal network with L=N=8 and B=1, two of six seeds acquire ICL; four converge slowly to a suboptimal minimum (2312.03002). Initialisation changes behavioural ICL-transience timing while data seeds have little effect; induction heads are not inspected across these seeds (2503.05631). The label-count delay sometimes vanishes across seeds (2404.07129). Lag-1 masking relocates the circuit in 2 of 3 runs (2609.15545).

method_sensitivity.factor: intervention timing, schedule and data source
method_sensitivity.what: The upweighting window decides between delay and acceleration (2510.12071). A gate fade gives zero-gate accuracy .734 ± .028, against .293 ± .128 for a hard switch at step 1050 and .097 ± .020 at step 600 (2609.10287). The starting checkpoint decides whether ICL emerges (2503.05631). In Pythia-160M, synthetic data guided by the 14M model gives +9.84%, against +2.56% for 160M-derived data (2601.21996).

At D=100, gradient descent stays on the induction-head plateau within 50k iterations while Adam escapes (2410.11474). On GMC, poor optimiser, learning-rate or batch choices can delay the transition or prevent convergence (2602.07562).

Training on bigram-distributed outputs reduces out-of-distribution in-context accuracy, while uniform outputs generalise, demonstrating training-distribution dependence (2306.00802). The books-mix comparison is confounded by out-of-distribution evaluation tokens, as the authors note (2404.19737). Path dependence is strong for associative recall; linear-regression ICL has a smaller fade advantage and can learn under forced-zero training. Unforced linear regression has normal MSE 0.0656 and zero-gate MSE 0.1296, establishing degradation without establishing disappearance of ICL. These task and setup differences support V5 (2609.10287).

Positional encoding affects whether ICL emerges (2503.05631). In two-layer attention-only toy models, formation takes 600 ± 0 steps with APE free and 940 ± 55 with RoPE free (2607.06621). In a 0.5M two-layer model at t<128, previous-token attention is 0.9513 with RPE, against 0.5460 with APE (2412.11459). In the multimodal decoder, RoPE yields lower ICL accuracy and a higher data-complexity threshold than APE; this comparison supplies no numerical formation time (2601.20796).

status_amendment.public_note: The status now explains how it treats one study in which model depth made no consistent difference to whether in-context learning fades, in a synthetic classification task: as a limit on which training-setup properties matter, not as grounds to call the claim contested. The level is unchanged at independently reproduced.
